parts: Lesson 22: Wave Phenomena and Light — Summary

A wavefront is the locus of all particles vibrating in the same phase, so the phase difference between two points on a wavefront is zero. Rays are normal to wavefronts. A point source gives spherical wavefronts, and a distant source or a source at the focus of a lens gives plane wavefronts.

Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, and the envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets gives the new wavefront. It explains reflection (i = r) and refraction (Snell's law).

Interference is the redistribution of energy due to the superposition of light waves from two coherent sources. Coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference. Two independent lamps are not coherent, so they show no steady pattern.
Phase difference = (2π/λ) × path difference; a path difference of λ/4 means a phase difference of π/2.
Bright fringe: path difference nλ (phase 2nπ). Dark fringe: path difference (2n − 1)λ/2.
Intensity: I_max = (√I₁ + √I₂)² and I_min = (√I₁ − √I₂)². Beams of I and 4I give 9I and I. Equal beams give 4I and 0. Intensities in the ratio 9 : 1 give I_max : I_min = 16 : 4 = 4 : 1.
Fringe width β = λD/d, and all fringes are equally wide. Halving d and doubling D makes β four times; tripling d makes it ⅓.
In a liquid of index μ, λ becomes λ/μ, so β falls to β/μ.
The number of fringes in a given width varies as 1/λ: 99 fringes at 6000 Å become 108 at 5500 Å.
White light gives a white central fringe with coloured fringes on either side.
Example: λ = 450 nm, d = 0.15 mm and D = 1 m give β = 3 mm.
Diffraction is the bending of light round obstacles or apertures comparable in size to its wavelength.
Sound (λ about 1 m) diffracts round walls easily, so we hear a horn round a corner. Light, with λ about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, does not, so we cannot see the lamp.

Single slit of width a: the central maximum has angular width 2λ/a and is twice as wide as the other fringes, whose intensity falls off rapidly. A narrower slit or a longer wavelength widens the pattern; the linear width grows with D.
Interference fringes are equally wide and equally bright; diffraction fringes are not.
Light can resolve objects comparable to its wavelength: a particle of 3 × 10⁻⁴ cm needs λ of about 3 × 10⁻⁶ m, i.e. ν of about 10¹⁴ Hz.
Polarization shows that light is a transverse wave; longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarized.
Ordinary light is unpolarized. A polaroid transmits only vibrations in one plane. Malus' law: I = I₀ cos² θ, so rotating one polaroid by 45° halves the intensity and by 90° cuts it to zero.
Polarization by reflection — Brewster's law: μ = tan iₚ. At the polarizing angle the reflected and refracted rays are at 90° to each other, and v = c cot iₚ. For μ = √3, iₚ = 60°.
Optically active substances, such as sugar solution, rotate the plane of polarization.
Uses of polaroids: sunglasses, 3-D films, anti-glare headlights and photographic filters.
Doppler effect for light: a receding star's lines shift to longer wavelengths (red shift), with v = cΔλ/λ. A shift of 0.032% means v = 9.6 × 10⁴ m/s.
